body:
## Module 7 in two minutes

Most legal training in this field teaches you the rules. **This module teaches the stack**, because the rules here move at different speeds, and **advice built on the wrong layer expires without telling you.**

What that costs: a practitioner who learned in 2024 that intrusive electronic monitoring was presumptively unlawful is **wrong today**, because the memorandum saying so was withdrawn. One who concludes from the withdrawal that the exposure is gone is **also wrong**, because the statute never moved. Same failure, opposite directions, not knowing which layer the proposition sat on.

**Five layers.**

**Statute — decades.** Section 7's protection of concerted activity, the duty to bargain over wages, hours and terms and conditions, *Weingarten*. Untouched by any of this.

**Board doctrine, flips with composition.** Decided cases. The Board changes its mind when its membership changes; that is how the agency works.

**General Counsel priority: fastest, rescindable overnight.** What the prosecuting arm will argue. Real, because it determines whether a charge becomes a complaint. Not a right.

**Rulemaking — a different clock**, undone by litigation, a successor administration, or Congress. A rule is not a decision, and commentary reports the two interchangeably.

**Contract, binds you regardless of who runs the Board.**

> **The question about any proposition is not "is this true?" It is "what is this true *of*, and what would have to happen for it to stop being true?"**

### Go and read your management-rights clause

**In 2019, in *MV Transportation*, the Board adopted a contract-coverage test:** roughly, if a change fell within the compass of a negotiated clause, the employer could act. **In December 2024, in _Endurance Environmental Solutions_ (373 NLRB No. 141, 10 December 2024), it overruled that and restored clear and unmistakable waiver**, the standard it had applied for some seventy years — **retroactively.**

Now the facts, because they are your facts. A waste-hauling company installed video cameras in a fleet of roughly **400 trucks** to monitor employees, without bargaining. Its defence was a management-rights clause reserving the right to *"implement changes in equipment."*

> **That clause was not enough.**

Your clause very probably contains a phrase of about that generality: equipment, methods, technology, systems, means of operation. **A Board has held that this class of language does not clearly and unmistakably waive bargaining over installing monitoring technology on people.** Your technology is more capable than a dash camera, and your clause is not more specific.

**And the trap.** The Board reached a 3–1 majority on **7 August 2026** that satisfies its own three-vote convention for reversing precedent, and commentary expects the unilateral-change standard to be among the targets. **That does not help a change you make now.** Doctrine in this line applies retroactively, so a change is judged under whatever standard exists when the case is decided. **Betting on a reversal is not a legal position.**

**Settled doctrine, unsettled application, and the distinction is the lesson**, because almost everything written about this collapses it.

**Settled:** a change to wages, hours, or terms and conditions of employment is a mandatory subject, and a mandatory subject cannot be changed unilaterally without notice to the union and a genuine opportunity to bargain. AI that monitors, scores, allocates, schedules or disciplines plainly touches terms and conditions.

**Not settled: there is no Board decision applying the duty to bargain to an AI deployment.** Not one. SAG-AFTRA's charge against Llama Productions, filed May 2025 over an AI-generated voice performance, alleges exactly that — **and a charge is not a holding.**

> **Secondary sources state the conclusion as though it were law. It is a strong inference from settled doctrine, with a pending charge and no decision.**

*Unverifiable is not the same as false*, and it applies to a legal proposition exactly as it applies to a vendor claim. The inference is strong enough to plan on. But a strong inference and a holding are different objects, and the difference shows up in three places: advising a leader who wants certainty, pricing the risk of being wrong, and whether you can cite anything if challenged.

**The practical answer does not depend on resolving it.** Under clear and unmistakable waiver your existing clause probably does not cover an AI deployment affecting unit work. **So bargain it, or negotiate language that says what you may do.** Both are available now. Neither requires a Board decision. And the second is what the other side of the table has been doing while this was argued about.

**The full module's most useful finding: while practitioners waited for a Board decision, unions negotiated the obligations directly.**

**Notice** is the most common form. CWA's agreement at the Microsoft subsidiary ZeniMax requires notice to the union when AI implementation affects bargaining-unit work, and became a template reused in tech. About **38% of union members report at least one contract provision on automated management or surveillance**, most often notice. **NewsGuild-CWA holds roughly 85–90 agreements containing AI language, 58 of them ratified**, not a pilot, a body of negotiated practice accumulating faster than the case law.

And the provision that should stop you: the **UPS–Teamsters** agreement **prohibits using sensor data as the sole basis for discipline and requires human review of context** before AI-generated performance data is acted on. **That is 101's assist-versus-decide line and this track's rung boundary, written into a collective bargaining agreement by the other side of the table**, enforceable by grievance and arbitration.

> **Notice, human review, and records** are the three duties the AI employment statutes keep landing on. They are also the three things unions are winning at the table. **In a represented workplace you may owe them years before a regulator asks**, and the enforcement is faster because it is a grievance rather than an investigation.

So: **your contract is an AI compliance document**, and somebody should read it that way on purpose rather than finding the provision in a grievance. And build notice, human review and a record into every deployment — you are then ahead of the legislation, inside most negotiated language, and defensible under the duty to bargain. **You do not have to pick.**

**Finally, why none of this is conditional.** Protected concerted activity does not require a union. Section 7 covers employees acting together about pay, hours or conditions in a workplace with no union and no campaign, and the rescission of GC 23-02 **removed the theory, not the section.** Concluding a non-union workplace is outside all of this is the layer error in its most expensive form: a statute assumed to have stopped applying because a memorandum was withdrawn.
